ui.flyThrough.title: Fly-through: from the state matrix into memory
ui.flyThrough.label.matrix.key: Round key 0 · 4×4 matrix, filled column by column
ui.flyThrough.label.matrix.state: State · 4×4 matrix, filled column by column
ui.flyThrough.diagramLabel: Diagram: 16 bytes move from the 4×4 matrix into the lanes of xmm0 and on into RAM.
ui.flyThrough.caption.matrix.rd_key: Round key 0 is the AES-128 key itself (FIPS 197, App. C.1: 00 01 … 0f). Like the state, it is read as a 4×4 matrix filled column by column: byte i sits in row i mod 4, column ⌊i/4⌋ (FIPS 197, §3.4).
ui.flyThrough.caption.matrix.out: The output block: after the last round the state holds the C.1 ciphertext 69 c4 e0 … 5a, read as a 4×4 matrix filled column by column: byte i sits in row i mod 4, column ⌊i/4⌋ (FIPS 197, §3.4).
ui.flyThrough.caption.register.c-ref: The C reference never uses xmm0: GETU32 packs every 4 bytes into one 32-bit word. The lanes show what a 128-bit register holds instead: byte i sits in lane i, so byte 0 lands in the lowest lane.
ui.flyThrough.caption.register.aesni: AES-NI keeps all 16 bytes in one register, byte i in lane i of xmm0: a 128-bit load (movups) puts them there. Byte 0 lands in the lowest lane, and the matrix becomes one flat row.
ui.flyThrough.caption.memory.rd_key.c-re: The C reference stores rd_key as four u32 words read big-endian with GETU32, so rd_key[0] = 0x00010203. A little-endian CPU writes the lowest byte first: each 4-byte word appears reversed in RAM (03 02 01 00 …).
ui.flyThrough.caption.memory.rd_key.aesn: AES-NI code stores each round key straight from the register (movups, the $movkey of aesni-x86_64.pl). RAM holds rd_key in the original byte order 00 01 02 … 0f; no word is reversed.
ui.flyThrough.caption.memory.out: The ciphertext stored to out[16] keeps its byte order in both implementations: PUTU32 in the C reference undoes the GETU32 swap, and AES-NI writes the register as it is (69 c4 e0 … 5a).
